subject: chemistry-hl
author: original (NevaIB)
title: Measuring enthalpy changes
bigPicture: Every reaction moves energy between the system (the chemicals) and the surroundings (everything else). If heat flows out, the surroundings warm up and the reaction is exothermic; if heat flows in, they cool and it is endothermic. Measuring the temperature change of water lets us put a number on it: the enthalpy change, ΔH.

keyIdeas.cue: What is the difference between heat and temperature, and what is conserved?
keyIdeas.answer: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference (J); temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles (K). Energy is neither created nor destroyed: what the system loses, the surroundings gain.

keyIdeas.cue: How do you recognise exothermic and endothermic reactions?
keyIdeas.answer: Exothermic: heat released to the surroundings, temperature of surroundings rises, ΔH negative (combustion, neutralisation). Endothermic: heat absorbed, surroundings cool, ΔH positive (thermal decomposition, dissolving NH₄NO₃, photosynthesis).

keyIdeas.cue: How do you draw and read an energy profile?
keyIdeas.answer: x-axis: reaction coordinate; y-axis: potential energy. Exothermic: products below reactants. Endothermic: products above. The hump is the activation energy (reactants to peak); ΔH is the vertical gap from reactants to products. Lower energy = more stable.

keyIdeas.cue: How is ΔH calculated from a calorimetry experiment?
keyIdeas.answer: Q = mcΔT, where m is the mass of the water/solution being heated (1 cm³ ≈ 1 g), c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and ΔT is the temperature change. Then ΔH = −Q/n, where n is the moles of the limiting reactant; convert J to kJ. Units: kJ mol⁻¹. Standard (⦵) means 100 kPa, a stated temperature (usually 298 K) and standard states. Heat loss to the surroundings makes experimental values less exothermic than literature values.

keyTerms.def: Everything else, including the water and the container.
Heat transferred at constant pressure, per mole of reaction.
Energy to raise 1 g of a substance by 1 K.
100 kPa, usually 298 K, substances in standard states.

workedExamples.title: Neutralisation
workedExamples.prompt: 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl is mixed with 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ NaOH; the temperature rises by 6.7 K. Calculate ΔH.

workedExamples.title: Combustion of a fuel
workedExamples.prompt: Burning 0.46 g of ethanol (M 46.08) heats 200 g of water by 12.0 K. Calculate ΔHc and compare with the booklet value (−1367 kJ mol⁻¹).
workedExamples.answer: ≈ −1.0 × 10³ kJ mol⁻¹; much less exothermic than the booklet value because of heat loss and incomplete combustion.

misconceptions.wrong: m in Q = mcΔT is the mass of the reactant.
misconceptions.right: It is the mass of the substance whose temperature changes (usually the water or solution).

misconceptions.wrong: If the temperature rises, ΔH is positive.
misconceptions.right: A rise means heat was released to the surroundings: ΔH is negative.

misconceptions.wrong: Heat and temperature are the same thing.
misconceptions.right: Heat is energy transferred (J); temperature measures average kinetic energy (K).

paper1A.stem: 100 g of water is heated by 10 K. Using c = 4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, how much heat is absorbed?
On an energy profile, what represents ΔH?

paper1B.data: Temperature–time data: a solution sits at 21.0 °C for 3 min, reagent added at 4 min; readings then fall steadily from 27.5 °C at 5 min to 26.0 °C at 9 min.
paper1B.prompt: Explain how to find the best value of ΔT from a graph of these data.
paper1B.answer: Extrapolate the cooling line back to the time of mixing (4 min) to correct for heat loss: about 27.9 °C, so ΔT ≈ 6.9 K rather than 6.5 K.

assessmentNote: Paper 1A = multiple choice, no calculator; Paper 1B = data-based questions (format from public sources, confirm with the official guide). All prompts here are original practice, not predictions of exam questions.

errorHints.hint: Use the total solution mass in Q = mcΔT, convert J to kJ, and divide by moles of the limiting reactant.
Get the sign right: temperature up → ΔH negative.
c for water is 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ in the booklet; use it unless the question gives another value.
State the main systematic error (heat loss) and its effect (ΔH less negative than literature).
